lessons.title: Nonplanetary Bodies in the Solar System

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Research for information on the movement of nonplanetary bodies in the solar system, for example asteroids and comets.
- Compare and contrast the movement of the nonplanetary bodies in the solar system.

pages.title: What is a Nonplanetary Body?
pages.body: A nonplanetary body is any object orbiting the Sun that is not classified as one of the eight major planets, and the solar system contains a wide variety of such bodies, each following its own characteristic path and behaviour. Asteroids, comets, meteoroids and dwarf planets are the main types of nonplanetary bodies studied at this level, and this lesson treats each one individually to understand how it moves and behaves within the solar system.

questions.q: A nonplanetary body is best described as
o: Any object orbiting the Sun that is not one of the eight major planets
Any of the eight major planets
questions.e: A nonplanetary body is any object orbiting the Sun that is not classified as one of the eight major planets, and the solar system contains a wide variety of such bodies, each following its own characteristic path and behaviour.

pages.title: Asteroids
pages.body: An asteroid is a small, rocky object, generally too small to be classified as a planet, that orbits the Sun. Most known asteroids are found in a region called the asteroid belt, located between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, where countless asteroids of varying sizes travel around the Sun in fairly stable, roughly circular orbits, much like the planets, though far smaller and more numerous. Some asteroids follow orbits that bring them closer to Earth, and these are studied particularly closely by scientists concerned with the small possibility of a future collision.

pages.title: Comets
pages.body: A comet is a small body made largely of ice, dust and rock, often described as a dirty snowball, that follows a highly elongated, stretched out orbit around the Sun, very different from the roughly circular orbits followed by planets and most asteroids. As a comet's orbit brings it close to the Sun, the Sun's heat causes some of its icy material to vaporise, releasing gas and dust that form a glowing head, called a coma, and often one or more long, bright tails that always point away from the Sun, regardless of the direction the comet is travelling. Far from the Sun, comets cool down again and become faint, inactive objects until their orbit brings them close to the Sun once more, sometimes only after many years or even centuries.

questions.q: Studying asteroids and comets closely is important partly because it helps scientists
o: Assess any risk of collision with Earth
Guarantee no space object will ever approach Earth
Prevent the Sun from producing light
Remove all small objects from the solar system
questions.e: Studying the movement of nonplanetary bodies has real practical importance, since scientists track asteroids and comets that could potentially come close to Earth, assessing any risk of collision well in advance.

pages.title: Meteoroids
pages.body: A meteoroid is a small fragment of rock or metal, generally much smaller than an asteroid, travelling through space. When a meteoroid enters a planet's atmosphere and burns up due to friction with the air, it produces a brief streak of light called a meteor, commonly known as a shooting star. If a meteoroid survives its journey through the atmosphere and lands on the ground, the remaining fragment is called a meteorite. Meteoroids move at very high speeds and generally follow paths determined by the gravitational pull of the Sun and nearby planets, occasionally crossing a planet's orbit and entering its atmosphere.

pages.title: Dwarf Planets
pages.body:
A dwarf planet is an object that orbits the Sun and is large enough to have become roughly round under its own gravity, but has not cleared other objects from the area around its orbit, unlike a full sized planet. Pluto, once classified as the ninth planet, is now recognised as the most famous dwarf planet, along with others such as Eris and Ceres. Dwarf planets generally follow stable orbits around the Sun, though some, like Pluto, have more elongated, tilted orbits compared with the more nearly circular orbits of the main planets.

[[pic:A diagram of the solar system viewed from above, showing the Sun at the centre, the roughly circular orbits of the planets, the asteroid belt shown as a band of small dots between Mars and Jupiter, a comet shown with a highly elongated, stretched out orbit extending far beyond the planets, and a small labelled meteoroid crossing a planet's orbital path.]]

Notice how differently each type of nonplanetary body moves. Asteroids mostly follow fairly circular orbits concentrated within the asteroid belt, comets follow long, stretched out orbits that carry them from far beyond the planets to close to the Sun and back again, and meteoroids travel on paths that can unpredictably cross into a planet's atmosphere.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Comparing the Movement of Nonplanetary Bodies

pages.title: Comparing the Movement of Nonplanetary Bodies
pages.body: Orbit shape, orbit location, and typical size are three useful features for comparing how asteroids, comets, meteoroids and dwarf planets move through the solar system. Asteroids generally follow roughly circular orbits concentrated in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets follow highly elongated orbits that can carry them from the outer edges of the solar system to very close to the Sun. Meteoroids follow varied, often unpredictable paths determined largely by gravity, and are generally far smaller than asteroids or comets. Dwarf planets follow stable, roughly circular or somewhat elongated orbits, similar in general character to planetary orbits, but are found in regions, such as far beyond Neptune, where they have not cleared their orbital neighbourhood of other objects.

pages.title: The Nonplanetary Bodies Compared
pages.body:
| **BODY** | **WHAT IT IS MADE OF** | **WHERE IT IS FOUND** | **HOW IT MOVES** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Moon, or natural satellite** | Rock, and ice on some moons | Around a planet | It orbits its planet in a nearly circular path, and travels with the planet round the Sun |
| **Asteroid** | Rock and metal | Mostly in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter | It orbits the Sun in a nearly circular path in the same direction as the planets |
| **Comet** | Ice, dust and frozen gases | It comes from the cold outer parts of the solar system | It orbits the Sun in a very long, stretched path. Near the Sun it grows a bright tail that points away from the Sun |
| **Meteoroid** | Small pieces of rock or metal | Throughout the solar system | It moves round the Sun. One that burns up in the air of the Earth is a meteor, and one that reaches the ground is a meteorite |

These bodies are alike in that all are held in their paths by gravity and none gives out its own light. They shine only by reflecting sunlight. They differ in size, in what they are made of and in the shape of their orbits. Halley's Comet, for example, returns to the inner solar system about once every 76 years.

pages.body:
> ✍️ **Try these on your own. The answers are in the notes you have just read.**

- State one similarity and two differences between a comet and an asteroid.
- What is the difference between a meteor and a meteorite?
- Why does the tail of a comet always point away from the Sun?

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Studying the movement of nonplanetary bodies has real practical importance, since scientists track asteroids and comets that could potentially come close to Earth, assessing any risk of collision well in advance. Space missions have also visited several comets and asteroids directly, providing valuable information about the early materials that formed the solar system, since these small bodies have generally changed far less over billions of years than the larger planets have.
